#4153. Pokémon GO's Duolingo Crossover Gives Language Learners a Shot at Shiny Lucario

Duolingo's green owl already has a reputation for making sure you don't forget your lessons. Now, it's offering Pokémon GO players a different incentive to open the app – a chance at Shiny Lucario.

Redeem a code for free Pikachu Crocs in Pokémon GO. Gengar and Jigglypuff avatar items are available with purchases of the corresponding Crocs.

Pokémon GO and Duolingo have teamed up for Duo's Pokémon Party, a limited-time event that rewards language practice with Pokémon-themed avatar outfits and special Timed Research. You won't get Lucario just for finishing a lesson, but completing lessons on seven different days will earn you a chance to encounter one.

The crossover began on November 17, according to the official Pokémon GO announcement, and you can take part regardless of which Duolingo course you're studying.

First, update Duolingo and join Duo's Pokémon Party in the app. Completing a lesson in any course earns your first reward, with more rewards available for studying on additional days. These include up to four Pokémon-themed suits for your Duolingo avatar. The suits are cosmetic rewards within Duolingo, not outfits for your Pokémon GO trainer. To get something in Pokémon GO itself, you'll need the research code.

The outfits include Poké Ball, Pokémon GO, Chatot, and Pikachu suits, so there's something to collect even if you aren't interested in the Timed Research. There's a catch with those rewards, though – they won't stay in your Duolingo wardrobe forever. Duolingo says the suits will expire on March 31, 2027, meaning you'll lose access to them even if you've already unlocked all four.

For the Pokémon GO reward, you'll need to complete at least one lesson on seven different days. They don't have to be consecutive, but seven lessons in one sitting won't count. Once you've met the requirement, you'll receive a code for the collaboration's Timed Research.

Redeem that code on the Pokémon GO Web Store's redemption page using the account linked to your game. The Timed Research will then become available in Pokémon GO.

You don't have to begin a new language course, either. If you've been working through one already, those lessons count toward the seven-day requirement. The important part is showing up on seven separate days.

The research carries the language-learning idea into Pokémon GO. You'll choose a language for the tasks, which will appear in that language rather than the one you normally use in-game. Professor Willow will offer hints if you get stuck.

Completing the tasks rewards you with XP, Stardust, and encounters with Pikachu, Meowth, Chatot, and Lucario. Each Pokémon comes with a special background and can appear in its Shiny form. A Shiny Lucario isn't guaranteed, of course, but it's a pretty tempting reward for keeping up with your lessons.

A Shiny Lucario isn't guaranteed, of course, but it's a pretty tempting reward for keeping up with your lessons.

There's also a language tag for certain Pokémon caught through the research. Tapping it on their summary page shows their names in different languages. It's a small detail, but at least the partnership brings some language learning into Pokémon GO rather than stopping at a promotional code.

There are three deadlines to remember. You must join Duo's Pokémon Party by December 21, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time. After joining, you have until December 29 at 11:59 p.m. local time to complete lessons on seven different days and claim your Duolingo rewards.

You'll also need to finish the Pokémon GO Timed Research and claim its rewards by December 31, 2026, at 11:59 p.m. local time. Redeeming the code alone isn't enough, so don't leave the research until the last minute.

I haven't kept up with my Duolingo lessons lately, but this might finally get me to resume them. Apparently, the chance of a Shiny Lucario is more motivating than another reminder from Duo.

And even if the Shiny hunt doesn't work out, seven days of lessons isn't a huge commitment. Whether I'll manage to keep the habit going after the event is another matter.

It's quite refreshing to be able to make some actual progress in a mobile title without opening my wallet. Thanks, Pokemon GO.

#4152. Void/Breaker Review – Chaos Is The Point

Many games tout impressive destruction systems under the hood, but few implement it as well as Void/Breaker. The ruin is visually spectacular, sure – who doesn’t love to watch buildings crumble because of your grenade or gravity-thrown explosives? But importantly, it’s a critical aspect of Void/Breaker’s roguelite design. Enemies caught beneath falling rubble become instantly staggered, and that’s your moment to kill. Grenades do this too, as do most items you throw at the hostile AI machinery trying to end your run, creating a vortex of shifting priorities as you dash, jump, and shoot at sequential staggered enemies in your sightlines. Countless weapon mods and permutations make fewer than a dozen weapons feel like hundreds in your arsenal, adding even more blissful chaos to the mix. Though it can be difficult at times, if you can see through the literal remains of your destruction, one of the year’s most engaging shooters awaits.

Void/Breaker wastes no time getting a gun in your hand. An AI voice in your head wants your help escaping a simulation where thousands of runners attempt to reach the end of multi-arena stages to defeat a boss. He asks that you simply follow the simulation’s commands; meanwhile, he uses the data you collect along the way to find new exits for you and him. The storytelling style is very reminiscent of Valve’s Portal. Something much larger is at play here, but it’s worth discovering for yourself.

This narrative framework supports the game’s roguelite structure. Mechanically, however, you enter various themed digital stages, from liminal spaces to beaches to snow-capped cliffs and more, and attempt to survive. Most arenas consist of a couple of starkly white structures that your grenades and thrown explosives can topple (ideally onto waves of enemies below). Learning the language of Void/Breaker means constantly scanning your field of view for explosives and structures practically begging to come down, and then eyeing neon-green bars above enemies that tell you they’re staggered and ready for a quick kill. Developer Stubby Games throws plenty of wrenches into this formula, like armored foes and electrostatic enemies you must melee first, and elite bots that will have you on the back foot, but for the most part, Void/Breaker’s formula is “Break stuff, then kill.”

The game emphasizes explosives and bringing buildings down, but your guns do most of the killing; you can only select one weapon per run. You choose from a pistol, shotgun, machine gun, sniper, and more, and each has its perks (though once I unlocked the SMG, I rarely picked anything else). There’s no sense overthinking your weapon, though, because the dozens of mods you pick up each run determine its effectiveness. As you pick up more schematics, the pool of mods you find in chests or drop from enemies expands, and soon your gun fires corrosive acid, electricity, fire, projectile missiles, and more. Not to mention, mods change how the gun fires, how much damage certain bullets do, recoil, accuracy, and just about any other stat you associate with firing a video game gun. Wild combinations are easy to create, and a unique mod-stacking mechanic that can double or triple effectiveness adds a light touch of puzzle design to this otherwise straight shooter.

Stubby Games smartly emphasizes player expression, never getting in the way of the zanier combinations available to players. The SMG I used to beat the final boss featured mods that made each bullet electric, shot missiles with each shot, covered each bullet in a destructive orb, and featured a ricochet perk that made each bullet bounce off walls and split into even more bullets. I’m thankful for mid-run saves because this SMG permutation, paired with an ability mod that let me throw infinite grenades for a limited time, filled my screen with so much destruction that the entire game crashed. I’d usually bemoan such a thing, but I couldn’t help but laugh. I pushed my PC to its limit with my on-screen chaos.

Boss fights leave a little to be desired – I rarely died because of their simple bullet-hell arenas. Instead, most runs ended because, after bringing down every structure around me, I’d get so lost in the chaos that I wouldn't realize I was stuck in debris while enemies swarmed my location. As stunning as it is to see so much happening on screen, it can be hard to understand what is going on during the most chaotic moments.

Between enemy-filled arenas en route to a stage’s end boss, you might find a shop to buy more mods, ominous obelisks with risk-reward propositions (gain a lot of health or lose half your health, for example), optional trials, and strange phenomena that transport you to different locations. These moments are quick breaks in between bouts of adrenaline-fueled shooter action that I always welcomed – enemies can be relentless, especially as new types are introduced in each stage.

The rest of the Void/Breaker package offers few genre surprises. You can upgrade various traits between runs, research new mod schematics to add to the random pool, purchase new weapons, and discover fun secrets. You can unlock shortcuts, glean in-world information from computer terminals, and hear intriguing dialogue barks from the AI partner who needs your help. It’s all standard stuff for the rogue genre, but if anything, its simplicity pushes you back to the meat and potatoes of this shooter.

Void/Breaker’s shorter runtime – I rolled credits at 12 hours – ensures nothing gets too repetitive in its roguelite structure, but an expansive endgame promises even more to engage with, like different run modifications you can enable to make an already chaotic shooter even more anarchic. I’ll certainly be running it back (again and again) to see what other disruptions I can bring to this AI-simulated adventure. It’s hard not to when destruction feels this good.

#4151. NASA pushes Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound

NASA is pushing the limits of helicopter flight on Mars, testing rotor blades at speeds once considered too risky. The faster these blades spin, the more lift they can generate, potentially allowing future aircraft to carry heavier scientific instruments and travel greater distances across the Red Planet.

During tests conducted in March at NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory (JPL) in Southern California, engineers successfully pushed the tips of experimental Mars helicopter blades beyond the speed of sound without causing them to break apart. The experiments took place inside a specialized chamber designed to reproduce the harsh atmospheric conditions on Mars. Results from 137 test runs could help engineers develop a new generation of more powerful aircraft capable of carrying scientific equipment.

"NASA had a great run with the Ingenuity Mars Helicopter, but we are asking these next-generation aircraft to do even more at the Red Planet," said Al Chen, Mars Exploration Program manager at JPL. "That's not an easy ask. While everything about Mars is hard, flying there is just about the hardest thing you can do. That's because its atmosphere is so incredibly thin that it is hard to generate lift, and yet Mars has significant gravity."

Ingenuity made history on April 19, 2021, when it became the first aircraft to achieve powered, controlled flight on another world. However, it was designed primarily to demonstrate that flight on Mars was possible, not to transport scientific instruments. NASA now hopes to go much further. Its recently announced SkyFall project, along with other potential future aircraft, could carry sensors and scientific instruments to investigate Mars from the air. Flying at low altitudes would provide valuable information to support future robotic and human missions.

Why Flying on Mars Requires Extreme Rotor Speeds

Helicopters generate more thrust by spinning their rotors faster or using blades with a larger diameter. That basic principle applies on Earth and Mars, but the Red Planet presents a much greater engineering challenge.

Mars has an atmosphere only about 1% as dense as Earth's, leaving helicopter blades with far fewer air molecules to push against. To produce enough lift, engineers must operate rotors at exceptionally high speeds, bringing their tips close to the speed of sound. Small rotors on Earth can also spin thousands of times per minute, but the denser atmosphere makes it unnecessary to push their tips toward supersonic speeds to generate substantial lift.

During Ingenuity's 72 flights on Mars, its engineers limited the helicopter's composite-skinned foam rotors to 2,700 revolutions per minute. This restriction served two important purposes. It kept the blades away from the complex and potentially unpredictable conditions near the sound barrier, and it provided a safety margin in case sudden winds (from a dust devil, for instance) caused the blade tips to move faster relative to the surrounding air.

"If Chuck Yeager were here, he'd tell you things can get squirrely around Mach 1," said JPL's Jaakko Karras, the rotor test lead. "With that in mind, we planned Ingenuity's flights to keep the rotor blade tips at Mach 0.7 with no wind so that if we encountered a Martian headwind while in flight, the rotor tips wouldn't go supersonic. But we want more performance from our next-gen Mars aircraft. We needed to know that our rotors could go faster safely."

The speed of sound also differs considerably between the two planets. At sea level on Earth, Mach 1 is approximately 760 mph (1,223 kph). On Mars, sound travels at roughly 540 mph (869 kph), largely because the atmosphere is much colder and consists primarily of carbon dioxide.

NASA Tests Supersonic Rotors in a Mars Simulation Chamber

To determine whether the new blades could safely reach these extreme speeds, Karras and his colleagues used JPL's historic 25-Foot Space Simulator. The rotor systems were developed and manufactured by AeroVironment in Simi Valley, California.

The researchers began with a three-bladed rotor designed for potential future Mars helicopters. After installing it inside the chamber, they removed the surrounding air and introduced a carefully controlled amount of carbon dioxide to recreate the thin Martian atmosphere. They then spun the rotor at progressively higher speeds while exposing it to simulated winds.

Because the experiment involved the possibility of a rotor breaking apart at supersonic speeds, engineers reinforced part of the chamber with sheet metal. The team monitored the experiment from a control room located just a few yards away, using instruments and a camera to track the rotor's performance.

The rotor eventually reached 3,750 revolutions per minute, bringing its blade tips to Mach 0.98, just below the speed of sound. Engineers then switched on a fan to produce headwinds against the spinning blades. With each successive test, they increased the wind speed to push the system further.

Breaking the Sound Barrier Boosts Lift by 30%

The experiments ultimately drove the rotor tips to Mach 1.08, surpassing the sound barrier and increasing the aircraft's lift capability by 30%. Crucially, the blades survived the supersonic conditions.

That additional lift could make a major difference for future missions. More powerful Mars helicopters could transport heavier scientific instruments, advanced sensors, and larger batteries, allowing them to conduct more ambitious investigations and remain airborne for longer periods.

Following the successful tests of the three-bladed design, the team evaluated a second rotor intended for SkyFall. This version has two blades that are slightly longer than those used in the first configuration. Because of their greater length, the blade tips could reach the same near-supersonic speed at a lower rotational rate of 3,570 revolutions per minute before simulated headwinds were introduced.

"The successful testing of these rotors was a major step toward proving the feasibility of flight in more demanding environments, which is key for next-gen vehicles," said Shannah Withrow-Maser, an aerodynamicist from NASA's Ames Research Center in Silicon Valley and member of the test team. "We thought we'd be lucky to hit Mach 1.05, and we reached Mach 1.08 on our last runs. We're still digging into the data, and there may be even more thrust on the table. These next-gen helicopters are going to be amazing."

Next-Generation Mars Helicopters Could Launch in 2028

Engineers working on SkyFall have already incorporated the new test results into the project's performance specifications. The findings provide an important foundation for designing helicopters that can operate under more demanding conditions while carrying substantially more equipment than Ingenuity.

Inspired by the historic success of Ingenuity, which remains the only rotorcraft ever to fly on another planet, SkyFall is designed to transport three next-generation helicopters to Mars in December 2028.

If successfully developed and deployed, these aircraft could expand the possibilities for exploring Mars, providing scientists with a new way to investigate the planet's surface and gather information from locations that may be difficult for traditional rovers to reach.

Materials provided by NASA's Jet Propulsion Laboratory. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

Lachesis is a great new support character. Her main job isn't just healing; it's making her teammates way stronger with powerful buffs. She's especially useful for tackling the game's hardest content.

Helena is a top‑tier DPS carry whose specialty is shield breaking and high AoE damage.

Hipper's a powerful new damage dealer who melts enemies with lightning and ice, but she's expensive to build and takes serious skill to play well.

Strong attacks (Astral Slash, Meteor Rush), plus invincibility and team damage immunity. Great for team builds, high damage, and tanky support. King - Scythe of the Crow

King is an amazing character who can shatter the opponent's shield and apply a damage-over-time effect. He also possesses one of the highest default attacks in the game. Of course, he is the main DPS unit that can also deal AoE damage to surrounding units, easily landing him at the very top of our Tower of Fantasy tier list amongst the best weapons. Nemesis - Venus

Nemesis can be an outstanding support unit that has the ability to heal up and further boost the damage dealt by attacks. She can deal AoE damage as well and provide useful heals to the entire team. Nemesis is currently one of the best supporters in Tower of Fantasy. Samir - Dual EM Stars

Samir, similar to King, has truly amazing DPS, which can shred through the enemies. She can paralyse and electrocute them, which further causes them to be unable to receive buffs. The overall damage potential of Samir is only outshone by the ability to fast-chain the skills, which can obliterate opponents extremely quickly. Crow - Thunderblades

Crow plays a very decent role when it comes to crowd control since his abilities not only deal a lot of damage but also can knock back opponents and paralyse them. He can also inflict more damage to low HP opponents while reducing the damage he takes.

Claudia can be an extremely fast damage dealer who can go invisible, and while she is able to greatly boost her damage output, she can also be fairly useful to the entire team. She works amazingly with Shiro and Nemesis, since that lineup can basically unlock her full potential. Cobalt-B - Flaming Revolver

Nan Yi (released in version 3.4) is a simulacrum that can be used both as a damage carry and a support. Her versatility makes her a valuable asset to have as she can fit in almost any team. Not only does she deal a good amount of damage to the enemies, but she also grapples them and buffs her allies.

Brevey is the latest Volt / Frost Benediction that was released on patch 3.5. She's arguably the best Support currently in the game. Meryl Ironheart

Meryl is a Vault character that can be used as a main DPS or a sub DPS. She has a variety of skills that can be used to deal damage, buff her team, and control the battlefield

Lana is a flexible Altered who helps from off‑field—she still does decent damage herself but mainly boosts the team with frequent assist hits and buffs. You can swap her element with the Evolution Cube; Cocoritter - Absolute Zero

With the ability to freeze enemies, heal and support allies, Cocoritter is one of the top-tier supports currently in the game, only beaten by Nemesis. She can create an area to fully heal allies, and, when using Swift Deliverance, she can also fully clear the user of all debuffs. However, she still has some flaws, and currently belongs just a bit lower than the top of the tier list. Tsubasa - Icewind Arrow

Tsubasa can stack up damage, increasing it by quite a lot. Once unleashed, she can inflict deadly shots while applying freeze and frostbite onto enemies. If she hits an enemy's weak point or lands a headshot, she can further boost the damage dealt to the target. Frigg - Balmung

Nola is a versatile physical DPS character. Her ability to choose any of the five elements grants her access to a variety of skills and abilities. She has a powerful ground attack chain and mobility, and she's overall a formidable force on the battlefield. While she can be challenging to master, Nola's strength and versatility make her a valuable addition to any team.

Asurada's main weapon, Hellfire, deals constant damage, and he summons afterimages to deal massive damage. His gameplay involves dodging, attacking, and using his afterimages to unleash powerful combos. He's a great choice for a fire team.

Huma ignites opponents and deals damage over time, but she can also knock the target back and gain damage reduction. Overall, she's a solid team tank if the situation requires one. Huma also has fairly short cooldowns, making her a good pick for certain scenarios. Ming Jing (Zeke) - Onyx Tortoise Attached Product Images

Ming Jing, also known as Zeke, is described as an unknown visitor from outside, and Domain 9 has welcomed this man with no past. He is often associated with the Onyx Tortoise, the weapon he wields. The Onyx Tortoise is an SSR-class greatsword with wide blades that can slash through foes. It is believed that the sword is too heavy to be picked up by mere mortals. Meryl - Rosy Edge

A tank hybrid with the ability to heal and inflict damage, Meryl can be quite fun to play in situations that require you to play something that needs some resistance or immunity to crowd control, as well as sustain. Zero - Negating Cube

Zero is a utility character that reduces the healing received by enemies, reducing their speed as well while granting allies and himself immunity. He can also heal allies, making him a versatile character. He is very viable, although he is officially in the middle of our ToF tier list. Shiro - Chakram of the Seas

Shiro is a Physical DPS unit that can cause lots of damage in short succession, being able to reset cooldowns and boost the damage dealt by allies.

Berry is a Physical/Flame support DPS unit that provides buffs to physical damage teams and sustain through healing on skill attacks. She excels when paired with fist-based main DPS like Nantou, offering team damage increases through her four-piece matrice set and final damage bonuses. Best performance achieved at A3 advancement for resistance shredding in end-game content, though her standalone damage output is underwhelming compared to dedicated DPS units. Recommended for team synergy rather than as a primary damage dealer.

She is a DPS unit that can apply grievous effects on the target, causing them to take additional damage. Can work well in some situations, but overall is not something you want to use constantly. Ene - Pummeler

Ene can taunt enemies and reduce the damage received, making her a pretty solid tank. She can also inflict crowd control effects, which makes her pretty good in situations that require you to have a front-line unit that can withstand an attack, or simply if you want to slow down the opponents with well-placed stuns. Pepper - Staff of Scars

Pepper can heal allies and has a decent dodge chance, automatically triggering said healing effect. She can also inflict some crowd control effects.

Can briefly paralyse the target, has a chance to grant allies attack boosting buffs (highly dependent on the chance to shatter the opponent's shield) - not too reliable in the long run. Hilda - The Terminator

Hilda can freeze the target and reduce their weapon charge rate, but even with all the damage increases granted by her skills, her damage output is still a little bit lacklustre in the long run. Can do well in the early stages of the game, though.

That's our complete tier list for Tower of Fantasy, with every weapon ranked! Do you have anything to add? Please leave a comment below!

#4149. The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time (2026) Review - Exceptionally Familiar

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time for the Nintendo 64 is the most important video game ever made… to me. My byline would not appear in the pages of Game Informer without my original experience playing that game. But it is nearly 30 years old, and despite establishing many important staples of 3D gaming, its age is becoming more apparent. Ocarina of Time was due for a re-examination, and its remake is a wonderful recreation of the 1998 experience with improvements on basically every element: visuals, storytelling, timeless design, and more. It is, however, a remake, and the coloring (though expertly done) is firmly inside the lines.

Ocarina of Time is gorgeous. That the game is less than 25 GB is an engineering marvel. I never quite came around to the odd looks of child Link or Zelda, but every other character, environment, enemy, item, and boss looks incredible. I eagerly looked forward to meeting every weirdo in Hyrule to see their new look, and was never disappointed. The ReDeads and Stalchildren are more traumatic than ever, and every NPC childhood crush I thought I had moved on from was reignited. Watching the sun rise and set over Hyrule feels as magical as it did in the past.

The same accolades can be awarded to the soundtrack. The new orchestrations are incredible, and watching Link’s 4K fingers play the proper notes on his ocarina is mesmerizing. Nintendo continues to fumble voice acting with stiff performances, but thankfully the vast majority of dialogue – one of the primary changes in this remake – is not spoken. Characters don’t necessarily have more to say, but what they say is more impactful, and there are a handful of small but exciting expansions to character and story details. Nothing is groundbreaking or changes how you look at familiar elements, but it manages to be simultaneously nostalgic and improved.

And that’s the closest I got to what I would debatably call a problem: It all looks new, but doesn’t feel particularly new. Ocarina’s overall design holds up. The time travel element is surprising and creates great opportunities to see the world change and evolve; puzzles and their solutions are rewarding; the basics of combat, though simple, are thrilling. All those elements have been adjusted, but not overhauled. Dungeons and their puzzles have been tweaked to remove annoyances (such as fewer keys in the Water Temple), and the new swordplay effects make connecting your blade to monsters feel incredible. But they’re all ultimately small changes that don’t cast Ocarina in a new light or consider its history. It’s a straightforward recreation. But an admittedly very good one.

The biggest, most impactful changes are the new full camera control and active jumping. Swinging the camera around to take a closer look at the upgraded environments is genuinely stirring, especially in the locations that used to be pre-rendered. There is an undefined and exclusive-to-video games emotion I experienced often while trekking locations I thought I knew so well, only to realize I have never seen or looked at it in this way, and I chased and captured that feeling all over Hyrule. Jumping may seem small, but it made me a more active participant in exploration. It also has the benefit of making some encounters feel somewhat trivial (turns out being able to jump over Blade Traps really diminishes their threat), and I was just fine with that.

The beautiful 2026 version of The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time does not study the legacy or impact of the landmark game on the video game medium. Instead, it is a meticulous and incredibly impressive recreation of one of the best games ever made. I was rarely surprised during my playthrough, but I was incredibly excited to see old friends and I happily share without embarrassment that playing through its final hour made me cry. For many like me, the original Ocarina of Time is an impactful adventure that arrived at a time in their lives when magic still felt real. Playing the game again 28 years later and appreciating the care taken to maintain and improve that original vision was the ultimate surprise of the whole experience: I didn’t expect to be so moved.

Alex Van Aken contributed to this article.

#4148. Nioh 3 launches, immediately becomes the most played Nioh ever on Steam

Just a few hours after launch, Nioh 3 is already the biggest release in series history on Steam.

It sounds like Koei Tecmo’s decision to finally release a Nioh game on PC day-and-date with PlayStation has paid off. The highly-anticipated Nioh 3 has gone live across both platforms, a first for a series that typically spends its initial release months as a console exclusive.

On Steam, and despite having only been available for just a few hours, the game has broken series records, and it continues to climb.

At the time of writing, Nioh 3 has peaked at 42,822 concurrent players on Steam (via SteamDB), and the number keeps going up. Because it’s in the middle of day in Europe and everyone is at work, it’s entirely possible - if not likely - that this figure will get much higher. A weekend bump is also possible, as we’ve seen with several recent releases.

As it stands, the current peak concurrent is enough to get the game in Steam’s top 20 most played games.

This already puts it ahead of all other Nioh games on Steam. The original Nioh peaked at 10,649 when it released in November, 2017. Nioh 2 fared much better, peaking at 41,325 concurrent players in February, 2021.

Of course, you could see that success coming a mile away. The game is currently number one worldwide in Steam’s list of top sellers. This is a jump of 46 positions, for a total of three weeks Nioh 3 has spent in that list.

There are many reasons as to why Nioh 3 has done as well as it has. Word of mouth coming off last year’s PS5-exclusive demo, and the more positive coverage that followed since are just two.

Just last week, Team Ninja released a pretty generous demo across both platforms, which has been well received by players, and likely contributed to sales, in no small part because progress in the demo carries over to the full game.

Critical reviews have been incredibly positive, too. We awarded the game four out of five stars, calling it “Team Ninja’s most accomplished action game, and the series’ most accessible.” It will be interesting to see what number the highest peak concurrent actually settles on over the weekend.

Until then, if you’re jumping in yourself, our Nioh 3 guides are essential reading. Start off with these useful and actually informative gameplay tips, and don’t start playing until you’ve changed these settings. Once you’re ready to get deeper, be sure to read up on how to play co-op with other players, and how to summon AI Acolytes to help you out.

#4147. A rare disease reveals a hidden flaw in the immune system

For decades, scientists believed they understood what caused the dangerous inflammation associated with a rare genetic disorder. Now, researchers at the Garvan Institute of Medical Research have uncovered evidence that challenges 30 years of established thinking and could open the door to a new treatment.

The condition, known as mevalonate kinase deficiency (MKD), can cause severe inflammatory episodes that are sometimes life-threatening. A new study published in Immunity identifies a previously underrecognized problem involving natural killer (NK) cells, immune cells that normally help the body eliminate infected cells.

The researchers found that these cells malfunction in people with MKD, setting off an excessive inflammatory response when infections occur. The discovery also points to a possible treatment using existing medications called JAK inhibitors, which could be particularly valuable for patients who do not respond to current therapies.

"This study has revealed a new target for this inflammatory disorder and sets the scene for future clinical studies to explore the use of JAK inhibitors or other drugs to neutralize interferon gamma in patients with MKD," says Professor Mike Rogers, Lab Head at Garvan and senior author of the study. "This could lead to a targeted treatment that hasn't been tried before."

Why a Rare Immune Disease Causes Dangerous Inflammation

MKD is a lifelong condition known to affect hundreds of children and adults around the world, although researchers suspect that many people with the disorder have never been diagnosed. Patients experience recurring attacks of high fever, skin rashes, joint pain, and inflammation in the abdomen. The most serious episodes can cause potentially fatal complications.

For roughly three decades, research into the disease has largely centered on macrophages, immune cells that help coordinate the body's inflammatory defenses. Existing treatments are designed to block an inflammatory signal released by these cells. However, approximately half of patients do not respond adequately, leaving a major need for better treatment options.

To investigate what might be missing from the prevailing explanation, the Garvan team examined blood samples from people with MKD and studied preclinical models of the disorder.

Their experiments revealed a significant defect in natural killer cells, which play an important role in the body's early defenses against viral infections. In MKD, these cells fail to mature properly and struggle to perform one of their most important functions: destroying infected cells before an infection can spread.

The consequences go beyond an impaired ability to fight infection. When natural killer cells cannot eliminate their targets, they release large amounts of inflammatory signaling molecules, activating other parts of the immune system and potentially triggering widespread inflammation.

"We found that these immune cells are essentially misfiring," explains Professor Rogers. "NK cells are loaded with toxic ammunition, stored in granules that are released to kill infected cells. However, in MKD these toxic granules can't be released from NK cells and remain trapped inside. When an NK cell fails to kill its target, it compensates by shouting for help, pumping out large amounts of interferon gamma - a powerful inflammatory signal. This activates other immune cells and causes the dangerous fever and widespread inflammation seen in patients."

Discovery Challenges 30 Years of Immune Disease Research

The findings suggest that natural killer cell dysfunction, rather than macrophage activity alone, plays a central role in driving MKD.

Dr. Marcia Munoz, Group Leader in the Rogers Lab and lead researcher on the study, says the results represent a major change in how scientists understand the disease.

"This really turns on its head 30 years of dogma about what was thought to be the underlying mechanism of disease. In MKD, the primary problem is in NK cells and not in macrophages, as previously believed," she says.

To investigate how this cellular defect contributes to the disorder, the Garvan researchers collaborated with Professor Mariapia Degli-Esposti and scientists at Monash University.

Using preclinical models, the team established a connection between malfunctioning natural killer cells and the severe symptoms associated with MKD. Their experiments showed that when the immune system cannot clear a viral infection, the resulting inflammatory response can cause extensive damage to organs.

These results help explain why a disorder involving defective immune defenses can also produce episodes of extreme inflammation.

Existing Drug Shows Promise for a New Treatment

The discovery has already helped guide an experimental treatment approach for a severely affected infant.

Working with doctors at the Royal Children's Hospital in Melbourne, the researchers explored whether baricitinib could reduce the excessive inflammatory signaling associated with MKD.

Baricitinib belongs to a class of medications known as JAK inhibitors. These drugs interfere with signaling pathways used by the immune system, including those involved in responses to interferon gamma. The medication is already used to treat other immune-related conditions, including rheumatoid arthritis and eczema.

Doctors added baricitinib to the infant's existing treatment regimen and subsequently observed an improvement in the child's condition. Inflammatory flare-ups became less frequent, and severe inflammation affecting the gastrointestinal tract began to heal.

Although the results from a single patient cannot establish whether the treatment will work more broadly, the improvement provides encouraging early evidence for a strategy that targets a different part of the inflammatory process.

The researchers believe their findings provide a foundation for future clinical studies investigating JAK inhibitors and other medications that block interferon gamma activity in patients with MKD, particularly those who have not benefited from standard treatments.

Discovery Could Help Explain Other Genetic Diseases

The potential implications extend beyond MKD itself.

Researchers have introduced the term 'prenylopathies' to describe a family of genetic disorders involving the same metabolic pathway affected in MKD. Early findings suggest that these related diseases may share a similar underlying problem involving natural killer cells that fail to function properly and instead generate excessive inflammatory signals.

If further studies confirm this connection, scientists may be able to identify common disease mechanisms and develop more targeted approaches to diagnosis and treatment across multiple disorders.

"Confirming this link could help end the diagnostic odyssey many patients endure for years or even decades before receiving effective treatment," says Professor Rogers.

Professor Mike Rogers is a Conjoint Professor at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney. Dr. Marcia Munoz is a Conjoint Senior Lecturer at St Vincent's Clinical School, Faculty of Medicine and Health, UNSW Sydney.

Materials provided by Garvan Institute of Medical Research. Note: Content may be edited for style and length.

#4146. 10 Ocarina of Time Remake Moments That Made Me Feel Like a Kid Again

Covering the video games industry since 2017, with experience in news, articles, and reviews. Currently a writer at DualShockers and gaming magazines.

Growing up with The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time means carrying a very special set of memories with you. I first played this adventure as a kid, when the idea of growing up, taking responsibility, and dealing with the more bittersweet aspects of life (just like Link) felt very different from what it does today.

Back then, I was simply a child exploring Hyrule, discovering secrets, and wondering what would happen next. Now, coming back to this world as an adult, I find myself looking at everything through a completely different lens (of Truth, I suppose!).

But despite seeing this adventure with more mature eyes, there were moments when I completely forgot about everything around me, and, for a few seconds, I wasn't a grown-up playing a remake on a modern console anymore. I was that same kid sitting on the floor of my bedroom, playing Ocarina of Time on a CRT television and getting lost in a world that felt magical. So, let's get a little nostalgic today and revisit the 10 remake moments that made me feel like a kid again.

I dare you not to shed a few tears when you hear the first notes of The Legend of Zelda's iconic main theme – it is that very moment when you finally realize this remake is real, and you're about to embark on a journey that has meant so much to you for so many years.

There's something incredibly powerful about hearing a familiar melody return with a fresh presentation. Suddenly, all those childhood memories come rushing back, and you remember exactly why you fell in love with this series in the first place.

Thankfully, the remake also brings enough improvements and new touches to make the experience feel fresh. It's a wonderful balance between revisiting something familiar and getting excited about discovering it all over again. And we're only at the title screen!

Some games have opening sequences that are simply too good to get old, no matter how many times you replay them. And I feel exactly that way about the introductory hours of Ocarina of Time. Running around Kokiri Forest, learning about this world through the eyes of its young inhabitants, and slowly figuring out what we're supposed to do is still a delight.

There's so much to love about this section: getting those cryptic instructions from Navi, finding the Kokiri Sword and Hylian Shield, and finally making our way into the Great Deku Tree. It does such a wonderful job of introducing the world and making us feel like we're part of this little community before the adventure truly begins.

Honestly, just thinking about it makes me want to grab a bag of snacks, sit on my favorite childhood beanbag, and spend another afternoon exploring the forest. Some things never change, do they?

I think we can all agree that this is a canon event for every Ocarina of Time player: leaving Kokiri Forest and immediately sprinting toward Hyrule Castle, desperately trying to reach it before nightfall. Otherwise, you'll find yourself surrounded by those creepy Stalchildren, and nobody wants that on their first trip through Hyrule Field!

Thankfully, that particular rush isn't quite the same in the remake, giving us a much calmer first experience with the enormous landscape. And while I love that frantic moment from the original, I have to admit that I really needed those few extra seconds to stop and appreciate the view.

Seeing Hyrule Field with this new presentation, taking in the scenery, and realizing just how far the world stretches ahead of us was surprisingly emotional. For once, I wasn't in a hurry to reach the castle. I just wanted to stand there for a little while and enjoy being back.

Some of the original's most charming quirks from Zelda: Ocarina of Time didn't make the journey.

Using the ocarina as a gameplay mechanic has always been one of my favorite things about the original Ocarina of Time. There's something special about learning a melody, remembering its notes, and realizing that you can use music to interact with the world around you.

Still, I had my doubts about whether the remake could recreate that same feeling – and, well, it did! Besides, there’s a new feature that lets us sing or even play an actual musical instrument to trigger a song makes the experience feel even more personal.

It's such a magical way to interact with one of the most iconic elements of the adventure, turning something we usually do with buttons into an actual musical experience, making every familiar melody feel a little more special.

That first moment when Link pulls the Master Sword from its pedestal is unforgettable. After spending so much time as a child, we're suddenly transported seven years into the future, and everything we thought we knew about Hyrule has changed.

But the real shock comes when we walk out of the Temple of Time and see what has happened to Castle Town. The once-bustling streets are now in ruins, the atmosphere is completely different, and the familiar kingdom has become a much darker place.

And seeing all of this with the remake's new visuals gave me chills all over again. For a moment, I felt the rush of running to Kakariko Village to check if everyone was still there – since it literally hit me like the first time.

One of the most enjoyable moments of playing as Adult Link in the original game is finally reclaiming Lon Lon Ranch from the terrible Ingo. After all that trouble, getting reunited with Epona, now fully grown, feels like such a rewarding moment. Playing Epona's Song, challenging Ingo to a race, and finally winning back the ranch is an experience I could never get tired of.

And the remake makes this moment just as magical as I remember it! I won't even tell you how many tears I shed during this sequence, especially when Epona makes that iconic jump over the fence, right above Ingo's head, to escape the ranch. That little moment brought the biggest smile to my face.

Having a horse in a video game was such a cool concept back then, and somehow, it still feels just as cool today. There's something incredibly freeing about riding across Hyrule with Epona by your side, and I don't think I'll ever get tired of it.

Nintendo has expanded one of the original Zelda: Ocarina of Time's most heartbreaking side stories.

The symbolism and challenge behind fighting Dark Link in the middle of the Water Temple already make this encounter memorable. You're facing a mysterious version of yourself in what is the most challenging dungeon in the entire game. But the remake somehow managed to make this already iconic fight even more impressive.

And if you've faced him yourself, you probably know exactly what I'm talking about! Dark Link can actually dodge one of your attacks by jumping onto your Master Sword and balancing himself on the blade. It only lasts a few seconds, but it's such an incredible detail that I couldn't help but stare in disbelief the first time it happened.

It's one of those moments when you're simultaneously nervous and amazed by what you're seeing. You can almost feel the tension through the controller as you try to figure out how to deal with this little menace.

I love pointing out how The Legend of Zelda titles occasionally pretend to be horror experiences, and Ocarina of Time has some particularly memorable examples. The Bottom of the Well is easily one of them, throwing Link into a disturbing underground area filled with fake walls and some of the most unsettling enemies in the game.

And let's not forget the ReDeads and Dead Hand! Seriously, who thought putting those things in a game for children was a good idea? I still remember how uncomfortable I felt exploring this place as a kid, never quite knowing what might be waiting around the next corner.

Returning to the Well with improved visuals didn't make things any less terrifying, either. If anything, seeing all those creepy details in greater clarity made the experience even worse. I was just as scared as I was all those years ago!

Eiji Aonuma and the development team for the Ocarina of Time remake discussed how one of the original's infamous dungeons is being improved.

Boss fights are one of the most memorable parts of any Zelda adventure, and Kotake and Koume are easily among my personal favorites. The twin witches offer a genuinely fun battle, but what makes them so special is how much personality they bring to the encounter. They're not just dangerous enemies, but also absolutely hilarious!

Their constant bickering, especially when they start arguing over which one of them is younger, never fails to make me laugh. It's such a silly little interaction, but it gives the two characters so much charm and makes the entire encounter even more memorable.

And the remake takes things a step further with dedicated cutscenes and voice acting, making the sisters even more entertaining. Their performances are spot on, and I found myself grinning like an idiot every time they started arguing.

Reaching the climax of Ocarina of Time is already an emotional experience, but climbing Ganon's Tower is one of those moments that stays with you forever. And I'll never forget ascending that final staircase before confronting Ganondorf, with the intense organ music gradually growing louder as we approach the villain.

But here's the brilliant detail: Ganondorf is actually the one playing that music! It's such a simple touch, but one that made players lose their minds back in the day, especially talking about a time when games weren't always experimenting with environmental storytelling in this way.

The remake recreates the moment beautifully, preserving all the tension and impact while giving us an even more impressive look at the scene. And then there's Ganondorf himself, and seeing his updated design in all its glory only makes the encounter more intimidating! It's easily one of my favorite interpretations of the King of Evil.

The Legend of Zelda: Ocarina of Time is one of the most beloved games of all time, but these remakes might be just as meaningful to fans.

#4144. Honkai: Star Rail Version 4.0 brings a new world, and a Fortnite collaboration

Honkai: Star Rail's next major update introduces a whole new planet to the RPG, and way more besides.

HoYoverse just wrapped up a big Honkai: Star Rail Special Program. We’ve been waiting for this one for a couple of weeks now thanks to a delay, but the developer has finally delivered all the news on Version 4.0, which will arrive February 13.

The upcoming major release is dubbed No Aha at Full Moon for a very good reason. Aha's Planarcadia is the big new world headlining Version 4.0.

Planarcadia is a place whose description sounds a bit like a Warhammer 40,000 Eldar homeworld, and is quite open about its cyberpunk inspirations. In-universe, however, it was born out of the pages of an art canvas, and it’s a world where pleasure is king.

The squad’s host in this chapter is Madam Pearl, who will oversee the the Astral Express’ return to the place where they first began their journey. Duomension City is where you’re going to land, and meet the creatures that dwell in this world.

The imagenae of Planarcadia require attention to survive, and they feed off people’s Wishpower. If they don’t get any attention, they perish, which does tie into the general themes of the place. Duomension City has other interesting locations that you’re going to visit, such as the Graphia Academy art school, the commercial district of Dovebrook, and a few other places hidden behind mysterious entrances.

The Phantasmoon Games is another highlight of Planarcadia, a competitive spectacle where you’ll have a chance to compete to become Aeon for a Minute. If you make it to the final stages, you may earn an audience with The Laughter.

Much like the world where the games take place, the whole point of the competition is to attract the most attention, so rules are a bit loose as to how you manage to do that. The event will bring together several of the game’s factions, though not everyone is there for the competition.

As you explore Planarcadia, if you have characters on your team who are on the newly-playable Path of Elation, you’ll earn Punchlines. The more you accumulate, the closer you get to catching Aha’s attention, which triggers Aha Instant.

Version 4.0 introduces two new 5-Star characters to Honkai: Star Rail. General Yao Guang (Madam Yao) is one, a Seer Strategist from the Xianzhou Alliance's Yuque. If you’ve been playing the game, you may already be familiar with her voice, as she's previously been in touch with our heroes via radio link. But V4.0 marks her first on-screen appearance, as well as her playable debut.

General Yao Guang is a Physical character on the Path of Elation whose specialty is using Weal and Woe Lots in battle, which she uses to increase Elation for allies, and grant everyone Punchline any time she uses a Skill. If an Aha Instant is triggered, she casts Woe Lots, which debuff enemies, causing them to take increased damage, all while regenerating Skill Points for the rest of the team.

Her aptly named Certified Banger buff adds one extra instance of Elation to teammates’ attacks. And her Ultimate grants the team Punchline, and triggers an extra Aha Instant.

The other new arrival is likewise a Path of Elation devotee. Sparxie is a suspiciously familiar streamer who uses her influencer skills in combat. When she fights, she turns the fight into a battle for attention, as she forces enemies to engage in a race for upvotes.

When you consume Skill Points, Sparxie will get gifts, which in turn cause her to regenerate Skill Points and Punchlines for the team. You can continue doing this to increase your damage. When Aha Instant is triggered, Sparxie unleashes a lucky draw that deals damage to enemies with each bounce.

She also benefits from the Certified Banger state, which causes the gifs she receives to deal more Elation damage to a random enemy target. Her Ultimate also deals more Elation damage.

Version 4.0 will see a few re-runs, too. Black Swan, Evernight, and Hysilens will be part of the first half's Warp events. The second half will see the return of Sparkle, Cerydra, and Rappa — that's right, HoYoverse have finally remembered Rappa exists, after one of the longest rerun waits in the game's history! Both Black Swan and Sparkle are getting a few tweaks to their kit with this version, too, so the timing works.

If you log in after launch, you’ll get 20 free pulls and a new free outfit for Ruan Mei. If you play while the Yao Guang fortune event is active, you could earn 1,600 Stellar Jades. You can also expect a free 5-Star character selector to arrive at some point after launch, giving you a free choice between popular (but admittedly a bit old for the meta these days) limited-banner characters Jing Yuan, Kafka, Dan Heng • Imbibitor Lunae, Jingliu, Sparkle, Acheron, and Aventurine.

Finally, the other major news is a Fortnite collaboration. Starting February 26, Kafka and Blade will join Epic’s battle royale shooter. On that day, you’ll find skins of the two Stellaron Hunters in the Fortnite Item Shop, and the new outfits are even compatible with Fortnite's LEGO styles. You can also expect other customisation bits like Back Bling, Pickaxe, and more to be part of the package.

If you download the game on the Epic Games Store, and take part in Honkai: Star Rail-themed activities, you’ll also get the Blade character outfit in Fortnite for free. Event schedule and timing will be announced at a later date.

#4143. Dead Cells weapons tier list - every weapon ranked

Not sure which melee weapon, ranged weapon, grenade, turret, or trap to bring? We've got you covered.

Updated on November 18th, 2026 - Version 3.5.15

Dead Cells has a lot of weapons, making it perfect for a tier list ranking every weapon. Throughout the game, you'll come across melee weapons, ranged weapons, traps, turrets, and even grenades, each with different effects like damage over time or freezing an enemy in their place. It can feel a little overwhelming, even though they're often slow or difficult to unlock and discover.

That's where our Dead Cells weapons tier list comes in. While we haven't gone into detail about most of the weapons here, we wanted to give you a quick overview of the best, the brightest, and, of course, most destructive tools in your arsenal to help you survive this perilous world.

Which weapons should you unlock in Dead Cells? It's a tough question, isn't it? You only have limited cells to spend on unlocking blueprints, so picking the best weapons to unlock can be tricky and overwhelming. We recommend starting with our S-tier weapons and working your way down from there. Most are ranked by their base damage numbers, but where a weapon or skill does something special and interesting, we've made sure to note it.

Of course, ultimately, it all comes down to personal preference. Make sure you read every weapon's description and decide if it would suit you. Some weapons have extra effects like applying a damage-over-time effect, like Bleed, or even combining with other weapons to create a one-two punch kind of effect. It's all personal. Dead Cells weapons tier list So, without further ado, let's get down to business. We've taken the time to break everything down by type for you: melee weapons, ranged weapons, shields (yes, they count), turrets and traps, and grenades. Each has its place in battle. Each will help you in some way to reach the end of the road.

If you disagree with anything on this list, then please let us know in the comments! These are a matter of opinion, after all, aside from their ranking on base damage. Critical damage is also important, so be sure to read the weapon description to take that into account.

Melee weapons make up the bread and butter of your arsenal, comprising everything from swords and axes to a spiked wrecking ball and a giant shark. Yes, a shark. Here, we've gone through and listed every melee weapon, ranked according to base damage.

Some weapons stand out more than others, of course. The Ferryman's Lantern allows you to kill an enemy to gather its soul. Then, as a secondary attack, charge it to fire those souls as projectiles, dealing critical hits if three souls are shot at the same time. With a base damage of 164 plus secondary damage of 107, then critical hits applying 429 damage, this is a monster of a weapon.

Others stand out for their usefulness and fun factor. With the Maw of the Deep, your third attack throws the shark, rooting the enemy and inflicting bleed. Rooted targets will then take critical damage - 158 base, and 270 critical.

The Rapier allows you to critical hit immediately after a roll or parry, and if you play the game like us, you'll be rolling around a lot anyway. With the Meat Skewer, your first attack places you behind the enemy, with your second hit applying critical damage. The Pure Nail comes courtesy of fellow Metroidvania Hollow Knight, allowing you to attack while moving left, right, and up. Drop down on an enemy and attack downwards to "bounce," just like in Hollow Knight, applying damage while in the air.

Finally, the Hard Light Sword is actually two weapons in one, along with the Hard Light Gun. A reference to the acclaimed Hyper Light Drifter, these weapons work in tandem. Fire the Hard Light Gun into enemies to damage and mark them. Then, the Hard Light Sword deals critical damage based on the number of shots it has received. Sword hits also recharge ammo for the gun, which (unlike other ranged weapons, more on those next) doesn't recharge over time. It's an elegant dance that might not be the most powerful, but is undoubtedly one of the most fun tools in the Dead Cells weapons arsenal.

Time for the first of our tier lists, then! Here we go: Rank Weapon S Ferryman's Lantern, Cursed Sword, War Spear, Tombstone, Flint, Oven Axe, Wrecking Ball, Giantkiller, Vampire Killer, Bible, Alucard's Sword, Death's Scythe, Misericorde A Toothpick, Symmetrical Lance, Shrapnel Axes, Hattori's Katana, Meat Skewer, Broadsword, Impaler, Crowbar, Twin Daggers, Hayabusa Boots, Vorpan, Shovel, Maw of the Deep, Rapier, Baseball Bat, Nutcracker, Pure Nail, Morning Star, Whip Sword, Sewing Scissors B Balanced Blade, Flashing Fans, Spite Sword, Rusty Sword, Bone, Swift Sword, Frantic Sword, Iron Staff, Assassin's Dagger, Rhythm n' Bouzouki, Seismic Strike, Wrenching Whip, Oiled Sword, Hayabusa Gauntlets, Blood Sword, Panchaku, Gold Digger, Machete and Pistol, Hard Light Sword, Giant Comb C Flawless, Sadist's Stiletto, Valmont's Whip, Torch, Abyssal Trident, Hand Hook, Spiked Boots, Bladed Tonfas, Dagger of Profit, Snake Fangs, Scythe Claw, Tentacle, King Scepter, Queen's Rapier, Starfury, Spartan Sandals

Ranged weapons are extremely helpful in Dead Cells, especially when you don't want to get close to an enemy. Most use ammunition that regenerates over time, or can be retrieved from enemies on death or following a successful parry, in the case of arrows. Some, like the combined Hard Light Sword and Gun mentioned on the previous page, have a special function - in this case, ammo doesn't recharge passively and instead must be recharged by landing hits with the Hard Light Sword.

Here's how we ranked the Dead Cells tier list for ranged weapons. Rank Weapon S Money Shooter, Ice Crossbow, Throwable Objects, Heavy Crossbow, Multiple-nocks Bow, Sonic Carbine, Barrel Launcher, Fire Blast, Magic Missiles, Medusa's Head, Anathema, Laser Glaive A Chakram of the Queen, The Boy's Axe, Peril Glyphs, Boomerang, Explosive Crossbow, Bow and Endless Quiver, Repeater Crossbow, Quick Bow, Laser Glaive, Gilded Yumi, Blowgun, Marksman's Bow, Ice Shards, Cross, Throwing Axe B Electric Whip, Lightning Bolt, War Javelin, Pyrotechnics, Nerves of Steel, Infantry Bow, Killing Deck, Hemorrhage C Beginner's Bow, Frost Blast, Ice Bow Firebrands, Hokuto's Bow, Magic Bow, Throwing Knife, Alchemic Carbine

Shields might be a boring choice for your adventure through Dead Cells, but don't sleep on them. Hold down a shield's assigned button to hold it up after 0.37 seconds. Attacks that hit the front are reduced by the shield's damage absorption percentage, typically around 75%, while also dealing damage to the enemy by the damage number listed on the shield.

Shields can also be used to parry attacks. Tap the button rather than hold it down, and it attempts a parry. If no attack hits during that window, you can't block or parry again for a little under a second. If your parry is successful, then a few things can happen: you can parry or block again immediately and enjoy an additional effect, depending on the attack.

Carrying a shield also passively creates a force field for 0.5 seconds after you take damage, absorbing most damage except DoT effects like poison and some enemy attacks.

Here, we've ranked shields in Dead Cells by their base block damage, meaning the damage the enemy takes after you block an attack. As always, read the shield's in-game description for any interesting effects, like AoE damage. Rank Weapon S Spiked Shield, Greed Shield, Punishment, Knockback Shield, Alucard's Shield A Force Shield, Thunder Shield, Assault Shield, Front Line Shield, Ice Shield B Rampart, Bloodthirsty Shield C Old Wooden Shield, Cudgel, Parry Shield

Deployable skills in Dead Cells come in three forms: traps and turrets, grenades, and various miscellaneous powers. It isn't possible to start with these skills without the Recycling Tubes upgrade.

First, let's cover deployable skills like traps and turrets. These come in powered and unpowered forms. Powered skills, such as turrets, need you to remain within their proximity for them to function. Line of sight is best, with the effective radius decreased if blocked by terrain. As long as you're within proximity, though, you'll notice a line of electricity connecting you to the deployed skill, allowing it to function.

Unpowered deployable skills are typically traps that don't actively attack on your behalf, such as traps that activate when the enemy steps onto them.

Let's rank the various types of deployable skills. First up, turrets. The Sinew Slicer is particularly worth noting. You'll come across it early, and it makes short work of early enemies without placing you in danger. Rank Skill S Barnacle, Scavenged Bombard, Heavy Turret, Cleaver A Double Crossb-o-matic, Sinew Slicer B Tesla Coil C Flamethrower Turret

Next up, traps and miscellaneous powers. The Emergency Door skill simply spawns a door in front of you, which acts like a regular door, meaning it can be destroyed to stun enemies on the other side. The Night Light is extremely situational and can be deployed in the Forgotten Sepulcher to help with the Darkness. Requiring 120 seconds to recharge, it can be thrown to a location to create a temporary light at that location. Touch it to replenish your light aura. Rank Skill S Crusher A Explosive Decoy B Wolf Trap C Night Light, Emergency Door

Grenades in Dead Cells do exactly what you expect: they explode. What more could you want? Simply throw, and enjoy! Some have added effects, of course, and can be paired with other skills or weapons for greater use. The Ice Grenade freezes enemies, for example, and the Root Grenade roots enemies, causing damage over time and keeping them rooted. The Magnetic Grenade is useful in crowded rooms. After a few moments, it attracts enemies in a large area, then explodes to deal electrical damage over time.

Grenades, like other skills, aren't exactly consumables as you would expect in other games. Rather they each have a set cooldown, meaning they can be reused over and over again.

The Hunter's Grenade is situational, which is why it's ranked C, but it's quite useful at the same time. Throw it to "annoy" a monster. When its health drops to 40% or less, use "Blueprint Extractor" to grab a blueprint. Rank Skill S Powerful Grenade, Holy Water A Infantry Grenade, Cluster Grenade, Magnetic Grenade B Stun Grenade, Ice Grenade, Fire Grenade, Root Grenade, Oil Grenade, Swarm C Hunter's Grenade

#4142. God Of War Laufey Delayed To May

PlayStation first-party developer Santa Monica Studio has delayed its upcoming action game, God of War Laufey, to May. More specifically, the PlayStation 5-exclusive title will now launch on May 20, representing a roughly three-month delay from the original February 16 release date.

"Since the reveal of God of War Laufey in June, we've been deeply grateful to see so much excitement for Faye's journey through the Everywhen," a statement from the studio reads. "We don't take for granted the trusted place in the studio to make an extraordinary experience worthy of the passion and dedication of our fans. With this in mind, we've made the decision to delay God of War Laufey's release to May 20, 2027. We will make the most of each moment until then by putting in the finishing touches and pushing the game to its fullest potential. On behalf of everyone on the team, we appreciate your patience and we'll be back to share more updates soon."

God of War Laufey stars Faye, Kratos' deceased wife from his Norse adventures, after she ends up in the mysterious realm known as the Everywhen following her death. There, she will fight monsters and creatures from various mythologies alongside a talking gelatinous cube and a talking sword sash. We'll have to wait a bit longer than expected now to see what her adventure entails.

God of War Laufey will now launch on PS5 next year on May 20. In the meantime, check out this newly revealed weapon, then read about how Amazon's God of War TV series has recast Kratos as Dave Bautista.
